t: the gathered ones. Those that are collected.

although they are from oral tradition, it says "it shall be put into water... a paradigm for all impure things that come into water". These laws were stated in the Sages' tradition in explaining the verses, and they can also be learned by the methods of exegesis transmitted to the Sages. And here they are learned by a paradigm (binyan av): for a vessel that became impure from a creeping thing, the Torah explicitly says that it is not purified until it is put in water, and from it we learn for all impure items.
the mat. A mat woven of ropes or reeds and the like (Hilchot Kelim 23:1).
even if he attached it to the ground. So that it became like ground, which does not become impure, nevertheless this does not remove it from impurity.
and even if he fixed it with a nail. He fixed it to a structure attached to the ground, whereby other vessels become pure (see there 26:1).
he filled it with plaster. In order to nullify its status as a vessel.
gypsum. Gypsum.
and glass vessels are like earthenware vessels. Since they are made from sand, like earthenware vessels (there 1:5).

because it is not a vessel with a receptacle, it is not included among the wooden vessels mentioned in the Torah. For the Torah says regarding impurity of creeping things (Leviticus 11:32) "of any wooden vessel... or sack," and the Sages learned that only a wooden vessel that receives things inside like a sack becomes impure (Hilchot Kelim 1:10).

it was included for midras impurity only. It is learned from the wording of the verse that a mat is also subject to midras impurity (see there 23:1), that is, it becomes impure if it is under a zav, zavah, niddah or a woman after childbirth (see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav u-Moshav 1:1, 7:1).
the law of the Torah. By Torah law it becomes impure only with midras, but by rabbinic law it becomes impure with all impurities (Hilchot Kelim there).
explicitly. In explicit words in the Torah.
in living water. Flowing water (Targum Onkelos, Leviticus 15:13).
all who are obligated to immerse. Such as a zav, a metzora, one who had relations with a niddah, and one impure from a corpse (Bavli Yoma 6b).
their immersion is by day. The time of their immersion is on the last day of their counting, and they do not need to wait until evening.
except a niddah and a woman after childbirth, whose immersion is at night. They must wait until the end of the days of their counting, and immerse on the night after completing the count.
as we explained regarding niddah. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:6.
and a ba'al keri immerses and goes about all day etc.. He may immerse immediately upon becoming impure, and even if he became impure at night he does not need to wait until morning.

as it says, "And it shall be toward evening he shall wash with water" etc.. This verse deals with the departure of a ba'al keri from the camp in the wilderness, and continues: "and when the sun sets he shall come into the camp." From this we learn that a ba'al keri can immerse throughout the day until evening, and when night comes he becomes pure.
and it is like his body by Torah law. The law of hair is the law of the body, so that if one hair remained outside the water, his immersion did not count at all.
for the water enters them. Enters under the clothes or penetrates them.
to become cold. To cool down.
but for terumah and sacred foods she is not pure until she immerses with intention. That she intend for the sake of purification for terumah or sacred foods (see Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tumot 13:2).
one who bends over. Who bends and gathers himself together.
whether the water entered all of it. In all parts of the body; for since he bent his body, he must make sure the water entered his entire body (Kesef Mishneh).

and one who says to his fellow, 'press down my hands on me in the mikveh,' this is disgraceful. For these ways look like playing rather than immersion, and there is also a concern of danger in them (see Kesef Mishneh and Toras Sefer Ha-Mikva'ot p. 28). Some explain that these ways are stringent practices, and he casts aspersions on those who immerse and do not follow this way (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 5:4).
the hidden places. Internal places in the body, such as the inside of the mouth or the inside of the nose (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 8:5).
and the folds. The folds of flesh (ibid.).
she rinses her folds in water. To remove interposing substances.
and a woman immerses in her natural manner. In her usual way.
like one weaving and like one nursing her son. For in these actions she spreads out her limbs and the water enters under the armpit and the like (see Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 9:12).
in the harbor. In the place where ships anchor.
he surrounded her with a mat. A mat standing as a partition on all sides.
for she is frightened and her immersion will not be valid. She fears falling, and perhaps she will not immerse properly (Kesef Mishneh).
a covering. A cover.
he is particular about it. The interposing thing bothers him.
and he did not pay attention to it, whether it was removed or not. It makes no difference to him whether it came off or stayed on.
a drop like a mustard seed. Like a grain of mustard.
these interpose for a person. Things that tend to stick to the body, which the person is particular about and wants to remove (see above 1:12).
mucus outside the eye. Discharge that accumulates in the lashes and corners of the eyes.
and a scab on top of a wound. Discharge that hardens around the wound on the outside.
and a medicinal substance. A healing material.
and a poultice. A bandage containing ointment (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eruvin 10:3).
and clumps of excrement. Excrement that has dried.
and specks. Grains of dirt.
and the mud of a pit. Mud from pits, which is thick.
and potters' clay. Clay of potters, which is less thick (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 9:2).
and mulberry sap. A white liquid secretion from the mulberry tree.

and all other saps, whether moist or dry, interpose. Because they are considered dirt from the fruit, and people are particular about them (Kesef Mishneh). Or because they stick more (see the notes of R. Saul Lieberman to Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 6:9).
that is attached to the flesh. Drawn along with it and stuck to it.
the dangling ones. Those torn from the body but not completely separated.

they interpose. Because they are considered detached from the body, and so the place where they connect to the body must be fit for the entry of water, and the dangling limb prevents this (Kesef Mishneh, who also brought another explanation, that despite their dangling they are considered part of the body, and therefore if there is an interposition on them, it invalidates).
it interposes until she first rinses. It interposes if she did not wash the place.
and dust. Secretions and dirt (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 9:2).
since she is not particular. It does not bother her if she is not clean in that place (ibid.).
the bandage. A dressing.
and the splints. Pieces of wood or metal used to hold a broken limb in place so that it heals.
and the bracelets. Bangles.
and the nose-rings. Ornaments of the ear and nose (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 11:8).
and the necklaces. Strings of beads worn around the neck (ibid.).
loose. Slack, so that water enters beneath them.
woolen threads etc.. See also Hilchot Shabbat 19:6. [Note: Maimonides in the Commentary on the Mishnah writes and vocalizes the word 'noy' (ornament) as 'noi'.]

because they separate the water from the body. And so they interpose (and are considered something the woman is particular about, since she tends to remove them when washing and the like - Rosh, Mikva'ot no. 25).
but hair threads do not interpose. Threads made of hair (see also ibid. halakhah 9).
threads on the neck. See also Hilchot Shabbat 19:10.
even of linen. Which tend to tighten more than wool (see Mishnah Mikva'ot 9:1).
for a woman does not choke herself with them. Rather she leaves them loose.

neck bands such as necklaces and chains... with which the woman chokes herself. Straps that encircle the neck, and tightening them against the body does no harm because they are smooth and wide (Rashi, Shabbat 57a).
so that she will appear fleshy. For by tightening, the flesh bulges out at the sides of the necklace, and this is regarded as an adornment for a woman, as it shows she is healthy and fleshy.
hair on the heart. Chest hair.
that became knotted and turned into tangles. That became entangled and stuck together by sweat and dirt and turned into a kind of braid (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 9:2).
when it is visible, it interposes. If the arrow protrudes outward, it interposes like anything on the body.
that is not visible. That is sunk inside the body.
and he eats his terumah. If he is a priest.
at evening. After nightfall (Hilchot Terumot 7:2).
even though it is an impure arrow. Since a swallowed item does not defile a person.
he became impure through its touch. The person became impure from his contact with the ring, since the ring was not purified by the person's immersion.
as we have already explained. Hilchot Tum'at Met 20:1-2.
in the cracks of his feet. Between his toes (Chazon Ish, Tosefta Mikva'ot 8:9).
plaster, poultice and bandage. Kinds of ointments and salves that are spread on dressings and placed on wounds.
as we have explained. Above 1:10.
and their ends. The tips of the hairs.

and pierced them and brought them out through the upper eyelashes. That hairs from the lower lashes grew upward toward the upper lashes, got tangled in them and passed through them outward (Aruch HaShulchan, Yoreh De'ah 198:90).
with the dust on his feet. With dust that stuck to his feet.
does not interpose. Because the water removes the dust (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 198:45).
who held his hands loosely so that water entered them. He held in a loose manner so that the water enters the thing he is holding.
and if he rinsed his hands in water. Before holding.
their immersion is valid. For the water on his hands joins with the waters of the mikveh.
one who carries her son behind her. Carrying him on her back.
and after she came up he fell. And therefore she did not know there had been an interposition.
that she clenched her hand. She tightened her fingers into a fist, so that water does not enter.
that she pressed her lips together. She pressed them firmly together.
she is purified from menstrual impurity. For the coins are not tightly held in the mouth and do not interpose. She is pure from her niddah state and permitted to her husband.

but she is impure on account of her saliva. She became impure through touching her own saliva, that is, saliva that was on the coins before immersion, since that saliva was not purified by immersion because it is considered detached from her (commentators on Mishnah Mikva'ot 8:5).

and she thus becomes first-degree impure, like one who touched the saliva of a niddah. For the saliva of a niddah is a primary source of impurity (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav u-Moshav 6:2), and the woman is now first-degree impure and defiles foods and liquids that she touches.
and these do not interpose for a person. Because generally he is not particular about them.
tangles of the head and armpit. Hair of the head and armpit that became entangled and matted (compare above, halakhah 7).
and the hidden places in a man. Tangles of a man's pubic hair (compare above, halakhah 3).
and mucus in the eye. Discharge that forms inside the eye due to illness (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 9:3; compare above, halakhah 1).
and a scab that the wound raised. Within the wound (compare above, halakhah 1).
and bits of excrement. Moist ones (compare above, halakhah 1).
and a dangling fingernail. That was partly torn off (compare above, halakhah 2).
the minor. Of a small child.
tied together in one knot. Tied together around themselves (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 198:5).
because the water enters them. For such a knot is by nature not so tight.
his immersion is valid. As with a minority that he is not particular about (above 1:12).
until the majority of his hair etc.. For when the interposition is on the majority, the immersion is not valid even if he is not particular about it (ibid.).

and it seems to me that a person's hair is regarded as his body etc.. In Maimonides' opinion hair is treated as part of the whole body, unlike the ruling of the Geonim, who hold that hair is judged on its own.
is regarded as his body. As part of the whole body.
as we have explained. Ibid.

it was Ezra's enactment that a woman wash her hair. By Torah law it suffices to check that there is no interposition (Bava Kamma 82a), and Ezra enacted that every woman immersing after her menstrual period wash and rub her hair.
and if it is possible to wash at night. On the night of immersion, for a niddah immerses at night (above 1:6).
with natron. One of the sodium salts used as a cleaning agent for laundering and washing.
it cuts off. Cuts hairs (and they tangle with the attached hairs).
with ahal. A plant of this name (crystal ahal) that is also used for laundering and washing.
it sticks. Glues and tangles.
with water heated by the sun. Water warmed by the sun.
they straighten the hair and make it flow. They smooth it and make combing easier.
they gather the hair together, bind it, and it becomes knotted. They entangle it and cause knots.
congeals. Hardens.

like a scab on top of a wound. Like a scab outside the wound, which interposes as stated above, halakhah 1 (Kesef Mishneh). It is not really like a scab, and therefore they were strict about it only regarding purities, as below halakhah 22 (see Beit Yosef).
and likewise mucus in the eye etc.. Although mucus inside the eye does not interpose, as above halakhah 14, nevertheless if it is dry it interposes regarding purities.
kohl. A blue substance used as makeup and for the treatment of eyes.
on top of the eye. Outside the eye.
fluttering. Opening and closing frequently (Rashi, Niddah 67a).
even on top of the eye it does not interpose. Because blinking removes the substance of the material (ibid.).
when does this apply. That the things listed from halakhah 19 onward interpose.
regarding purities. That if she touched purities they became impure.
for a convert at the time of immersion. When a gentile immerses for conversion (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 13:13).
and an interposing item was found on him. After some time had passed since the immersion.
even though he was handling that kind of thing all day. After the immersion, and there is room to claim that the interposing item stuck to him only after the immersion.
leave the impure person in his impurity etc.. We leave him in his state until proven otherwise.

and these interpose in vessels. That if they stuck to a vessel that requires immersion, they must be removed before immersion, since they interfere with a person's use and he is particular about them (see above 1:12).
and in the flask. A vessel with high walls and a narrow mouth (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 30:4).
on the inside they interpose. For the liquids inside them may become soiled by them (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 7:4).

from the craftsman's shop. They are new and attractive, and when there is a little dry pitch on the outside, it does not interfere with use and does not much spoil the vessel's appearance (ibid.). Some explain that the craftsman is not particular about the cleanliness of the vessel since the buyer will clean it anyway (Toras Sefer Ha-Mikva'ot p. 40).
from the householder. Used vessels.
on the outside they interpose. For the pitch spoils the vessel's appearance, and a person is particular about this and wants to remove it (Chazon Ish, ibid.).

on the serving bowl and the dish. Vessels used for hot foods (unlike the cup and flask, which are cold drinking vessels), where a person is particular even about dry pitch on the back of a vessel from the craftsman's shop, since heat melts the pitch and the one holding the vessel gets dirty (ibid.).
myrrh. A liquid with a pungent smell used as a perfume (Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 1:3).
and komos. A dye made from resin of a blackish shade.
both on a cup and on a flask etc.. For myrrh and komos do not dry, and one holding the vessel gets dirty even with a cup and flask, which are used for cold things (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 7:4).
the board. A plank used as a table.
the ladder-stool. A small stool used to climb onto a large chair.
the soiled ones. Dirty ones.
and on that of a poor person. Who is not particular.
a saddle. A saddle made of wood (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 9:5).
and on that of the zakakim. On the saddle of the zakakim, who make leather skins and carry them on the saddle and are not particular about its cleanliness (ibid.).
the saddle-cloth. A riding cushion placed on a donkey's back.
on both sides. If a great deal of dirt is absorbed in it so that it is visible on both sides of the saddle-cloth (Rash, Mikva'ot 9:6).
even on one side. If the dirt is on the surface only and is not absorbed in the thickness of the cloth.
for they are particular that their clothing be clean. See Hilchot De'ot 5:9.
pitch workers. People whose work involves handling pitch.
potters. Makers of earthenware vessels.
tree pruners. Who cut dry branches off a tree.
they do not interpose. For the dirt on their kerchiefs comes from their work, and they are not particular about the dirt whether it is removed or stays (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 9:7).
a butcher. A slaughterer.
fat. Grease.

on the inside of the sandal. And on the outside of the sandal it does not interpose, since people are not particular about this because it is the nature of the outside to get dirty (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 7:3).
on top. In the sandal's leather above the sole of the foot.
and underneath. In the leather beneath the foot.
on the bench... underneath. On the area facing the ground, where people are not particular about cleanliness.
and in the chair. A special chair used by dignitaries.
the fixed ones. Those attached to the chair or the cathedra.
and the wool in the necklace. A 'shir' is a bracelet worn on the neck, and when it is hollow, a piece of wool or the like is placed inside it (Rash, Mikva'ot 9:7).
and in the bell. A small bell.
the handle of the axe. Its handle.
covered. Overlaid.
as we have explained. Above 1:12.
that he put them in. Into the mikveh water.
not in their usual way. In a way that the water does not enter the cavity of the handle (for example, with the open side of the handle facing down, as explained in the next halakhah).
and did not shake them out. He did not move his hand to get the water into the cavity of the handle (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 10:1).
that were metal and became broken. That the parts of the handle were crushed against each other, and the water does not enter the crushed places (ibid.).
that he turned its mouth downward. That he immersed it with the open side down.

for the water does not enter all of it. For the air remains inside the vessel and prevents the water from entering (ibid.); therefore it must be immersed with its mouth facing up or with the vessel tilted on its side.
it is not pure until he tilts it on its side. So that the water enters all the places in the vessel.
a flask whose mouth sinks inward. Whose rim is bent into the vessel.
inkwells etc.. An inkwell bent greatly inward; for the water to enter all of it, tilting it is not enough but one must pierce it.
the necklace on it. A band on its neck.
they immerse it in its place. Without removing it from the animal, for when it lies loosely on it, the water reaches all its sides.
the kettle. A vessel for heating water.
with the coals in it. Together with the extinguished embers left in it.
he stirred. He moved the coals with his hand so that they would not cling to one side of the vessel and form an interposition (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 9:2).
as if he had not immersed. Because the liquids interpose between the vessel and the waters of the mikveh.
the water and the vessel are purified together. Since the water is purified in the mikveh, it does not constitute an interposition between the vessel and the mikveh water.
for water has purification in a mikveh. Unlike other liquids.
as we have explained in the laws of impurity of foods and liquids. Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 2:21.
we regard it as if it were water. For human urine is considered water (ibid. 10:2).
water of purification. Water into which the ashes of the red heifer were put, to sprinkle on one impure through a corpse.

and as if they were other liquids. In this case the water of purification is considered like other liquids and not like water, since its sanctity gives it importance and it is not nullified relative to the mikveh water unless the mikveh water is greater than it (Rash, Mikva'ot 10:6).

whose inside is pure and whose outside is impure. For example where the outer side of the vessel touched an impure liquid and thereby became impure with rabbinic impurity (see Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ot 7:3).

they follow the majority... since its impurity is rabbinic. With rabbinic impurity they were lenient that the white liquid whose color is not prominent is nullified relative to the greater quantity of mikveh water and does not interpose.
jugs. A jar.
moist mud. Wet, soft mud into which water can be absorbed, which is not considered an interposition.

and the mud was sinking into the water. The mud on the jug touches the water inside it, and when he immerses the jug, the mikveh water touches the mud and makes contact with the impure water (see Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 7:2).
the mud of a pit. Mud from pits, which is thick and interposes.

ordinary knots in poor people's garments, but if he was particular about them they interpose. A knot in a poor person's garment is generally made for mending the garment and it is assumed it will remain tied (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 10:3). Therefore such a knot is considered natural to the garment and does not interpose, unless the owner of the garment made known that he is particular about the knot and does not want to leave it.
householders. People who are not poor.
ordinary ones interpose. For it is to be assumed that the owner of the garment does not want to leave the knot.
the fringes of garments. Threads at the edges of the garment.
and the sandal straps. Loops of sandals.
and the tefillah. Tefillin.
for the casing. The tefillin boxes themselves, without the straps.
is attached to the strap, in the strap's housing, and is firm. Firmly connected by leather stitching to the strap housing in the casing (the place where the strap passes through the casing).
that does not move up and down. Tight on the strap and does not move easily (ibid.).
and the handles of. Gripping handles.
the water skin. A leather skin.
the shepherd's bag. A shepherds' leather pouch.

the ties at the openings of the robe that are made as loops. The open place in the robe that is tied in a loop after putting on the robe, and a button is inserted in it (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 10:4 and Kelim 29:1).
he must stretch it. Remove its folds in the water, because the sides of a sheet tend to fold.
and the loop of a sandal. A strap that goes into a loop.
for he will eventually open them and stretch them. At the time of use, and therefore he must open them and stretch them before immersion in order to immerse them in their natural state.
and of the olive press. Of an oil press where oil is made.
if they were firm. If the branches from which the basket is made are tightly bound.
he must pick out. Remove by hand the refuse between the branches.
he must shake. It suffices to shake and the refuse falls out by itself.
the water must enter them. Into their inner cavity, since the stuffing is not fixed in them but it is customary to remove it and put it back.
a round cushion. A cushion with no opening for removing the stuffing.
and the last. A mold on which a shoe is sewn, made of leather with soft material inside (Rash, Mikva'ot 10:2).
and the amulet. Parchment on which charms are written, covered with leather.
when they are laundered. And still wet.
until they bubble. Until certain places in the garment rise above other places, like blisters (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 10:4).

and stop bubbling. When the garment is dry before immersion, the stopping of the bubbling is the sign that the water entered all of it. But when the garment is wet, the mikveh water joins the water inside it, and there is no need to wait until the bubbling stops (Rabbi Ovadiah of Bertinoro and Tiferet Yisrael there).
to cut them. To cut them off.
he immerses them up to the place of measure. Up to the place where the handle is going to be cut, for anything about to be cut is considered cut (Chullin 73a).
the chain of a large bucket etc.. See also Hilchot Kelim 9:15.
and a small one, ten handbreadths. For a small bucket needs a longer chain.
for the water enters it. For if it does not enter, the large vessel has not been properly immersed, as above, halakhah 12.
and since it was valid etc.. Since the large vessel is purified by this immersion, it does not separate between the mikveh water and the inner vessels.

and if he tilted it on its side and immersed etc.. Some explained that this speaks of tilting the large vessel on its side so that water enters the small vessels while part of the large vessel remains outside the water, and so one cannot say that since the immersion was valid for the large vessel it was valid for the small vessels (Tosafot R. Yehuda he-Chasid, Chagigah 22a, cited in Toras Sefer Ha-Mikva'ot p. 20; Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot Tinyana 3:3). Many explained that even if he put the entire large vessel in, the immersion was not valid for the small vessels (see Beit Yosef, Shach and Taz, Yoreh De'ah 201:9, and for the reason see Mikveh Taharah no. 28, Gidulei Taharah question 13).

like the tube of a water skin. A hollow reed placed in the mouth of a leather skin for drinking and the like, whose measure is a diameter of the width of two average fingers (below 8:6), which is the measure of connection between mikva'ot. When the large vessel is open to this extent, the water that enters it is considered part of the mikveh water and itself purifies the small vessels, and therefore the purification of the small vessels does not depend on the purification of the large vessel.
for terumah. For the purpose of eating terumah, and all the more so for unconsecrated food.
for holy things. For use with offerings.
as we have explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ot 12:1.
as it is said, 'a gathering of water'. Wherever it is gathered (Leviticus 11:36). The Torah was not particular about the manner in which the water was gathered.
at a height of three. A height of three cubits.
drawn. Water that was drawn with a vessel.
a mikveh of undrawn water into which three logs of drawn water fell invalidated everything. When it has less than forty se'ah (below, halakhah 6).
three logs. About one liter.

they derived it by analogy etc.. They found a basis for it in the Torah's text from the fact that the verse equates the purifying gathering of water to two things: a natural spring and a pit of drawn water. The Sages learned from this that a valid mikveh is a kind of mean between them: if it contains drawn water it is invalid, but if it has only some human involvement ('human handling') it is valid, as will be explained below.
to dry them. To let them dry out.
he tips them over. He tilts them to pour out the water without lifting them.
for he did not fill them by his hand. And did not intend that they fill.
and poured. Poured out.
the gutter. A channel made in a way that it is not classed as a vessel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 4:1; and see below 6:6 for when a pipe is considered a vessel).
at any time and in any season. Whether when there are clouds or not.
when the clouds gather. When there are clouds, for clouds are like a pipe that is presumed to pour water.
these are valid, as if he had placed them on the roof to dry. As with one who places them on the roof (above, halakhah 3), who may break the jugs or tip them over.

he placed them when clouds were gathering, and they dispersed, then gathered again and the jugs filled, they are valid. Because his first intention was nullified when the clouds dispersed, and he is regarded as one who placed them at a time of dispersing clouds.
and if he broke them or tipped them over... they are valid. The water is valid provided he broke or tilted them and did not lift them, as above, halakhah 3.
a pot. An earthenware vessel in which he keeps the lime.
and it filled with water. That mikveh water entered it.

that only a little remained in the mikveh... he must break it etc.. The commentators pointed out that this law contains two stringencies relative to the law of one who places jugs on the roof to dry (above, halakhah 3): that some of the water must remain in the mikveh and not in the vessel, and that he must break the pot and not tilt it. As for the reason for the difference, it is explained that in the halakhah here the plasterer intended somewhat to draw, since it is the way of a pot to receive lime and water, and the plasterer brought it to the mikveh in order for it to receive; whereas the one who places jugs for drying has the opposite intention (Beit Yosef and commentators on Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 201:43).
to season them. So that they absorb water in their walls, and thereby will not absorb wine that is put into them (Kesef Mishneh).
and they filled with water. Mikveh water was absorbed in the walls of the jugs and also entered them.
for the mikveh absorbed its water. That water was absorbed in the walls of the mikveh.

and no water remained there at all... he must break the jugs. In this case the one who arranged the jugs did not bring them for receiving in them (unlike the plasterer above), but on the other hand he brought them for absorption in their walls (unlike one who places them for drying). Therefore in this case one stringency was required: that he break the jugs and not tilt them (Beit Yosef and commentators on Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 201:43).
and they descended to the lower mikveh. They went down into an empty pit lower than the full pit.
exactly. Precisely.

and likewise one may add a se'ah and remove a se'ah, and it remains valid up to its majority. Until a majority of the water that was in it originally remains. But if he added twenty se'ah of drawn water and removed twenty se'ah from the mikveh, it is invalid.
into the mikveh from the vessel. Directly.
he fills and draws outside the mikveh. He takes water in vessels and pours it outside the mikveh near it.
the channel. A pipe made in a way that it is not classed as a vessel (see below 6:6).
and put into it less than twenty. He added to the rainwater a little less than twenty se'ah of drawn water, so that altogether it is forty se'ah but invalid, as above, halakhah 6.
since the majority there was valid. For at first there were twenty se'ah and a bit of rainwater.
and this requirement. In the Talmudic discussion (Temurah 12a).
for they said at the end, 'drawn water that was channeled, all of it'. From the conclusion of the discussion one can infer that they permitted it even when all the water is drawn and channeled.
and according to this one's words. According to the opinion of some of the sages of the West.
this is a valid mikveh. Even though it was made entirely of drawn water.

and we never saw anyone who acted on this. We never saw anyone who relies on the view of some of the sages of the West, for what they said in the Gemara that drawn water that was channeled, all of it, is valid, should be interpreted as a case where initially there were twenty se'ah and a bit of valid water, as in the previous halakhah (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 4:4).
into a hollow. Into a pit.
steps. Stairs.
and they descend into the cave. And there they gather and rest.
if the majority is valid, it is valid. As with drawn water that was channeled.
they flow into the mikveh. Directly without channeling.
and if not, it is invalid. For three logs of drawn water invalidate valid water that does not contain forty se'ah, and they are not nullified by a majority (as above, halakhah 6).

a mikveh into which three logs fell etc.. The rule in this halakhah and the next is that three logs of drawn water invalidate the mikveh only if they fell in a single falling or something like a single falling, in which case they have significance; but if the fallings are completely separate, what fell first is nullified and does not combine with the next falling.
to increase. To enlarge.

three logs of drawn water into forty se'ah. So that together with the three logs there are altogether forty se'ah (Kesef Mishneh, based on the explanation above 4:6 that forty valid se'ah are not invalidated when drawn water is added to them).
that they poured. Poured into the mikveh.
and one who wrings out his garment and lifted it. A person who laundered his garment in a mikveh and lifted the entire garment from the water; all the water in the garment became drawn.
and the water in it falls from many places. From different sides of the garment, and altogether three logs fell into the mikveh.
the spout vessel. A drinking vessel from which one pours through a strainer made in its mouth (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 3:3).
these invalidate. For all these cases are regarded as a single falling.
a leather pillow or cushion. That have an open side and can hold water.
exactly. Precisely.

once he lifted their rims out of the water, the water in them becomes drawn. If he takes them out of the water with the open rim facing up, the mikveh will be short of forty se'ah, and the water in the pillow cannot be returned since it has become drawn.
and he lifts them by their bottoms. In a way that the sewn bottom side faces up.
and the basket. A basket.
and they lift them in the usual way. Because they have many holes, so the water in them is not considered drawn (see also below 6:8).
a mikveh that has etc.. An empty pit with three hollows in its walls one above the other, and in each hollow a log of drawn water (Tiferet Yisrael, Mikva'ot 2:5).
before they reach the third hollow. Before the water level reached the height of the highest hollow.
and if not, it is invalid. For the three drawn logs were mixed with the valid water before forty valid se'ah had accumulated.
because none of them was called by the name of invalid. Since none of them by itself became invalid, as three logs did not fall into it, therefore even when they combine they are not invalidated.
and the channel. A channel of flowing rainwater (for a channel of flowing spring water purifies drawn water by contact; Kesef Mishneh).

it is always invalid until it is calculated etc.. It is not enough that water equal to the amount of drawn water that was in it left the pit, since some of the outgoing water is rainwater, and so one must calculate proportionally. For example, if there were ten se'ah of drawn water in the pit and twenty se'ah of rainwater entered it (double the amount of drawn water), and fifteen se'ah of mixed water left, we estimate that the water that left contained ten se'ah of rainwater and five se'ah of drawn water. It turns out that five se'ah of drawn water remain in the pit, and it is still invalid (Tiferet Yisrael, Mikva'ot 3:3).
until it is known that the twenty se'ah that were in it left. Twenty se'ah of rainwater that had been invalidated.
and five kavs and more than a quarter of a kav. From a se'ah of drawn water that fell. For a se'ah is six kavs and a kav is four logs, so what remains of the se'ah is less than three logs.
and he mixed it with this invalid mikveh. He made a connecting point between them called 'hashka'ah' (contact; see below 8:7). In this way the valid mikveh purifies the invalid mikveh.
one who pushes the mud to the sides. Who moves the mud from the bottom of the mikveh to its sides.
and three logs were drawn from it. Three logs of water came out of the mud.
this is valid. For as long as he did not lift the mud and take it out, the water in the mud is not considered drawn.
and separated it from the mikveh to its side. He took out the mud and put it on the edge of the mikveh (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 2:6).
these invalidate. For when he lifts the mud by hand and separates it from the mikveh, the water in it is considered drawn (ibid.).
they made a mikveh at the outset. They channeled forty se'ah into an empty pit.
a troop. A group of soldiers.
and sprinkled. Splashed.
three logs. Of valid water.
this is valid. Although the water reached the mikveh by animal or person, it is not considered drawn, since it happened in the course of their movement without intention (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 3:3).

this is valid for challah, for terumah and for taking from it for the hands. For the mikveh water did not become impure from the impure water that fell into it, since water in the ground becomes impure only by intention (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 15:1). And although the mikveh water does not purify the impure water, nevertheless the impure water is very little and therefore there is no need to be concerned about it.
and invalid for making a mikveh upon them. The water that fell does not count toward the forty se'ah of a mikveh (see also below 7:4).

rains fell and increased upon them, they are valid for making a mikveh upon them. For when the rains increase they purify the impure water (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 15:2), and since they were purified regarding impurity, they were purified regarding mikveh and complete the forty se'ah.
this is invalid for challah, for terumah and for taking from it for the hands. Because three impure logs is a significant amount.
and invalid for making a mikveh upon it. The mikveh is invalidated, and adding to complete forty se'ah will not help, for all the water in it became drawn (as above, halakhah 1).
they are valid for challah, for terumah and for taking from them for the hands. For they were purified by the rains, as explained in the previous passage.

and invalid for making a mikveh upon them until all the first waters leave... and less than three logs of them remain. Like the law of a mikveh into which drawn water fell and became invalid and afterward valid water was added to it (above, halakhah 6).
and likewise a mikveh that has forty se'ah less a dinar, and three logs of impure drawn water fell into it etc.. This case has the same law as the case mentioned in the previous passage.
and invalid for making a mikveh upon them. Until all the first waters leave, all of which became drawn, as stated in the previous passage.

just as it was purified for immersion, so it was purified for everything. For when the mikveh has forty se'ah of valid water, it is valid for immersion and even purifies the impure water that fell into it (this halakhah has been explained according to Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 1:7; and see Kesef Mishneh, who explained it differently).
vessels that receive. That can hold liquid.
that water flowed over them. Flowed through them.
provided they are made for receiving. As explained in the next halakhah.
pipes. Tubes.
that are wide in the middle and receive. A pipe that widens in the middle and then narrows again, a shape that creates a capacity to receive in the wide place.

they do not invalidate the mikveh. Because the wide place in the middle of the pipe was made so that the water would emerge from the narrow place with pressure, and not for receiving in it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 4:3).
a trough in the rock. A hollow carved into a rock that is attached to the ground.
does not invalidate the mikveh. The water flowing from the trough into the mikveh is valid for immersion.
but a vessel that he attached to the rock. A trough that was made as a detached vessel and which he afterward attached to the rock.

he pierced it from below or from the side like the tube of a water skin, it is valid. If he pierced the trough he had attached to the rock with a hole about two fingers wide (see below 8:6), he nullified its status as a vessel.
a kneading trough. A vessel for kneading.

and pierced it with a hole that purifies it. A hole that nullifies it from vessel status regarding susceptibility to impurity (Kesef Mishneh). Some explain that this means a hole that removes it from being considered a vessel for the purpose of drawing, namely a hole like the tube of a water skin mentioned in the previous halakhah (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 4:6).
and likewise if he plugged the hole with lime and building. With lime and small stones and the like, like a construction, and did not attach the vessel to the ground.

it does not invalidate. For to nullify its status as a vessel one must pierce the vessel, and in addition perform an act of building, such as attaching to the ground or plugging the hole in the manner of building.
he plugged the hole with lime and gypsum. Lime and gypsum, which is not a way of building.
and if he moved it over the ground and over the lime. He dragged the vessel over them so that building materials would stick in the hole.
and smeared it with mortar on the sides. Around the hole, to make the building materials stick firmly to it.
this is valid. For this too is an act of building (Kesef Mishneh).
a board. A plank.
a rim. A frame on all sides so that it can hold liquid.
he stood it up. He set it on its side at a slant.
for he did not make it for receiving. He did not set it up in a manner that receives in it but so that the water would rinse it and flow on.
one who digs in a pipe a place to receive the pebbles that roll in the water. Who digs a hole in the middle of a pipe so that the small stones in the water gather in it.
and it hardened like gypsum. That is, the earth was packed tightly in the hole and plugs it firmly.

and they fell into the mikveh. In a way that the water was not poured into the mikveh but remained absorbed in the sponge, or remained inside the bucket, for example where the bucket's mouth is narrow (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 6:4).
the chest. A wooden box or cupboard (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 15:1).
unless they were pierced like the tube of a water skin. In which case the water in them is considered mixed with the sea water and is valid like it.
a basket. A basket.
they immerse in them. Because they have many holes and the water in them is mixed with the sea water.
the water drawn from them does not invalidate the mikveh. For it is not considered drawn.
a gistera. A potsherd that serves as a base for catching liquids under large vessels (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 2:6).

were purified from their impurity. For the water in the gistera is connected to the mikveh water (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 6:6; some explained that the connection arises because part of the gistera's rim is slightly lower than the mikveh water - Kesef Mishneh in the name of the Rosh).
as long as they are in the airspace of the gistera. While they are between the walls of the gistera that protrude above the water.
the water on top of them. The mikveh water above the immersed vessels.
from the airspace of the gistera. For an impure earthenware vessel defiles liquids that are in its airspace (see Hilchot Kelim 13:3).
and it again defiles them. The water that became impure defiles the immersed vessels (see ibid.).

and his hands are impure from the airspace of the oven. For when the one immersing comes out of the water he is in the cavity of the oven, and the Sages decreed that the airspace of an earthenware vessel defiles the hands (Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ot 8:1).

unless the water was above the oven at the height of his hands etc.. That the oven is sunk in the water, and the height difference between the water and the oven is the height of the immerser's hands, so that his hands are outside the cavity of the oven and within the water.
for earthenware vessels are not purified in a mikveh. And therefore the oven remains in its impurity although it is sunk in water.
as we have explained. Above 1:3.

his immersion was not valid. The commentators found this law difficult, since drawn water becomes valid when connected to sea water (as above, halakhah 8), and they resolved it in different ways (see the Rishonim on Makkot 4a). Some explained that this speaks of one immersing in order to eat terumah (as follows from the continuation of the halakhah dealing with a loaf of terumah), for there is a special stringency here regarding the eating of terumah (see Meiri there and Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).
and a loaf of terumah that fell there. After the person's immersion.

it became impure through the drawn water. Which was defiled by the person (but a loaf of unconsecrated food did not become impure, since regarding unconsecrated food the drawn water was made valid through contact and has the law of the rest of the sea water, Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).
since they flow. Flow well.
drawn water that was beside the mikveh. Water in a vessel placed beside a mikveh that has less than forty se'ah of valid water.
for they are like a mikveh next to a mikveh. They are considered separate from the valid mikveh.
the drawn water was in the middle. In a vessel placed in the middle of the mikveh.

they invalidate the mikveh. The contact between the invalid water and the valid water invalidates the valid water, because the invalid water is in the middle of the mikveh and is regarded as mixed with the valid water.
one above the other with a wall between them. One next to the other with a shared wall in the middle, except that one is higher than the other.
if opposite the hole there are three logs of drawn water. If the water in the pool of drawn water located opposite the hole, across the width of the pool up to the outer wall, amounts to three logs.

the upper one is invalidated, because the hole is as if it were in the middle of the upper one and not at its side. Since the pools are open to each other, the water opposite the opening is considered mixed with the valid water in the upper one, as if it were in its middle (based on Mishnah Acharona, Mikva'ot 6:11).
how large must the hole be to contain three logs. How does one calculate the volume of water between the hole and the wall opposite it in order to know whether it contains three logs.

if the lower pool was forty se'ah, the hole must be one three-hundred-and-twentieth of the pool. In the calculation proposed here, one measures the area of the hole relative to the area of the wall in which it is located, and if the hole's area is one three-hundred-and-twentieth of the area of the wall of the mikveh in which it is located, it contains three logs.
for a se'ah is six kavs and a kav is four logs. Altogether twenty-four logs to the se'ah. So forty se'ah contain nine hundred sixty logs, and three logs are one three-hundred-and-twentieth of that.
and one of them is drawn, from the side. One of the three contains drawn water and is at one of the sides.

and drawn water does not invalidate a mikveh that has forty se'ah, as we have explained. Above 4:6. On the contrary, the two mikva'ot with valid water combine into one valid mikveh of forty se'ah, and it validates the mikveh with the invalid water (as below 8:7), and therefore all who immerse are pure.
a mikveh is not invalidated by a change of smell or a change of taste. For even foul or bitter water not fit for a dog to drink is valid for immersion (compare Hilchot Berakhot 6:9).
by a change of appearance. The color of the water.
from the waters of any fruits. Liquids squeezed from fruit.
for they said only drawn water. And not another liquid, even drawn.
and a log of wine or fruit juice fell into it and changed its appearance, it is invalid. Until its appearance returns to the appearance of water, as in halakhah 9 below.
some complete the mikveh. There are liquids whose falling into a deficient mikveh helps complete it to the measure of forty se'ah.
they invalidate and do not complete. There are liquids whose falling into a deficient mikveh invalidates the valid water in it.
they neither complete nor invalidate. There are liquids whose falling does not change the mikveh's law.
and frost. A kind of very fine snow (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 7:1).
and ice. Water that freezes on the ground or on the surface of a body of water (ibid.).
and pourable mud. Thin, sticky mud like saliva (ibid.; some explain it as soft mud that can be poured from one vessel to another - Rashi, Sukkah 19b and others; and see below 8:9).
in a hollow. In a pit.
and pickling liquids. Water in which fruit or vegetables were pickled.

and boiling liquids. Water in which things were boiled. Although these liquids have some resemblance to fruit juices, their law is the same as any water, and they invalidate the mikveh because of the prohibition of drawn water.
and temed. Water that was left on wine lees or grape refuse so that it absorbs the taste of wine.
before it fermented. Before fermentation.

and these neither invalidate nor complete etc.. For the Torah required 'a gathering of water' (Leviticus 11:36), and therefore liquids that are not water are not considered part of the mikveh, neither to complete it to the measure nor to invalidate it with three logs.
other liquids. Oil, wine, milk, blood and honey (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:2).
and brine. The liquid extracted from salted fish (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nedarim 6:4).
and muries. A seasoning made of various things, especially fish pickled in salt (ibid.).
and temed after it fermented. For after fermentation it is considered diluted wine.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.
and sometimes these complete the mikveh. There is a particular case in which the liquids mentioned in the previous halakhah complete a mikveh to the measure.
valid. For a mikveh is invalidated by a change of appearance only when another liquid is mixed into it, as below, halakhah 12.

dye water etc.. Water colored with a certain color is still called water and therefore has the law of all water, since color is something without substance and does not turn the water into another liquid (based on Makkot 3b).
olive dregs. A black liquid extracted from olives.
and if the mikveh had forty se'ah of valid water. Which is not invalidated by pouring drawn water into it (as above 4:6).

if it does not have the appearance of water that has not changed, to the extent of forty se'ah, one may not immerse in it. If the mikveh does not contain forty se'ah that have not changed, it is short of the measure and one may not immerse in this mikveh at all.

and one who immerses in the place that changed, his immersion is not valid. Even in a case where there are forty se'ah that have not changed, one may not immerse in the part of the mikveh that changed (for its connection to the forty se'ah that did not change does not make it valid for immersion).

they invalidated it only if they changed its appearance. Because this mixture is called 'diluted wine' (Makkot 3b), and therefore its law is that of wine, which does not invalidate by drawing but only by change of appearance, as above, halakhah 1.

and they fell into the mikveh, they did not invalidate it etc.. For three logs of drawn water invalidate the mikveh only when all three logs are water. But if they are mixed with another liquid, even if their appearance is that of water, they do not invalidate.
whose water changed its appearance on its own. For example, many people immersed in it and the water turned dark.

they said only that it changed because of another liquid. The law of change of appearance derives from the requirement that a mikveh contain water and not another liquid (based on Sifra Shemini, parashah 9, ch. 10, halakhah 1), so that when another liquid changes the appearance of the water, it is like a mikveh containing another liquid. But if the mikveh contains only water whose appearance changed, this is not a change of appearance that invalidates.
the connected one. The joined one.
those next to the mouth of the mikveh. Those outside the mikveh pit, adjacent to it.
and the places of the hoofprints of animals. Hollows formed by animals' treading.
if they were connected with the mikveh water like the tube of a water skin. If there was a crack the width of two fingers (see below, halakhah 6) connecting the hollows to the mikveh pit.
one may immerse in them. When the water in the hollow covers the entire item to be immersed, such as a small vessel.
the chambers of the cave and the cracks of the cave. In their time most mikva'ot were in caves, and in the walls of the cave there were hollows and cracks that could hold a little water.

but by any amount. And there is no need for a width of two fingers, because the holes are inside the space of the mikveh and are considered part of it, unlike the hollows in the previous halakhah, which are outside the mikveh and are considered a separate place (like a small mikveh next to a large mikveh).
steps. Stairs.
and he was moving the water back and forth. The person moved the water with his hand and created waves.
once the wave passed over it, it is pure. For the wave is joined to the mikveh and purifies like a mikveh.
a hollow within the mikveh. A pit beneath the floor of the mikveh.
sound and able to stand. Stable, so that when the immerser stands on it, it does not give way (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 6:1).
one does not immerse etc.. For the hollow is considered a separate place.
that cracked lengthwise. That has a crack from bottom to top along its entire height (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 6:9).
they combine. They are considered one mikveh, as if the wall were not there.
and if it was in both. Together.
it cracked crosswise. Cracked from side to side horizontally along its entire length.
until it is in one place like the tube of a water skin. For the wall still separates, and two mikva'ot can join only through a hole the width of the tube of a water skin.

like a garlic peel across the width of a water-skin tube. Since the connection is not in the middle of the wall's height but above the wall and open to the air, there is no need for a hole that is like the tube of a water skin on all its sides (as explained in the next halakhah); it suffices that the width of the hole is like the water-skin tube and its height is any amount.
and they turn in it. That the fingers can turn around inside the hole.
the first two fingers etc.. The ones next to the thumb (the index finger and the middle finger).
anything that stands in the water-skin tube reduces it. Anything inside the hole causes the hole to be considered blocked at that spot.
from the creation of water. For example green algae on the surface of the water and creatures that form in water (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 6:7).
they do not combine. The mikva'ot.
for its measure is halakhah. The Torah's measures are law given to Moses at Sinai, and are not stated explicitly in Scripture (Eruvin 4a).
they purify the upper mikveh from the lower. An invalid mikveh can be made valid by connecting and touching it to a valid mikveh, even if the valid one is lower than it.
and the far from the near. Even if there is distance between the mikva'ot.
lead. Lead.
for pipes do not invalidate the mikveh. As above 6:2.

and he places his hands under it. He presses with his hands on the water when the end of the pipe is in the valid mikveh so that the water reaches the entire length of the pipe (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 6:8).
and draws it and makes contact. He draws the pipe with the water in it to the invalid mikveh and creates a point of contact.
in a stream. Descending on a slope.
the lowest and the highest, of twenty twenty se'ah. The lowest hollow and the highest hollow each contain twenty se'ah.

for flowing water does not connect unless it stands still. Rainwater does not purify when it flows and does not rest in one place (below 9:8), and in such a state it cannot create a connection between mikva'ot.
soft mud etc.. This is the 'pourable mud' mentioned above 7:3 (see Zevachim 22a).
bends down. Stoops.
is measured with the mikveh. Completes to the measure of forty se'ah.
one may immerse in the mud and in the water. One may immerse even if part of the body is sunk in mud.

in this soft mud over which the water floats. Soft mud from which a cow drinks completes to forty se'ah, as in the previous halakhah, and if the water floats over it, it is permitted even to immerse in it, since the immerser's feet are immersed in water before sinking into the mud (Tiferet Yisrael, Mikva'ot 2:10).
one may immerse in the water but one may not immerse in the mud. The water is considered a complete mikveh by virtue of combining with the mud, but one may not immerse in the mud.
yachbushin. A kind of worm that teems in water (some read 'yavchushin').
one may immerse in it. Since it is considered water.
in the eye of a fish. For example where its eye is very large and the fat in it turned liquid and contains the measure of a mikveh (based on Rashi, Zevachim 22a).
exactly. Precisely.

for the water fell short of forty se'ah. Since a little water is on the body of the first, and although his feet still touch the water, the water on his body cannot be regarded as connected to the mikveh.
a thick sagos. A thick woolen garment that absorbs a lot of water.

for all the water is connected. The water absorbed in the garment is considered connected to the mikveh, since the whole garment is saturated with water and the water in part of it that touches the mikveh water is connected to the water in the rest of its parts (unlike a person coming out of a mikveh, whose water does not cover him continuously - Kesef Mishneh).
even though he pressed down the legs of the bed etc.. For the narrow mikveh does not cover the bed unless the bed's legs sink into the mud.
in thick mud. Which is not considered part of the mikveh (as above, halacha 9).

for they did not sink into the mud until they had first been immersed in the water. The legs of the bed sank into the mud only after mikveh water was already on them, so the mikveh water covered the entire bed.
a pot. A cooking pot.
because the water spurts out and leaves. Because of the weight of the pot and the way it is lowered into the water.
he lowers it by its mouth. With the open side facing down, so that water enters the interior of the vessel and does not spurt out (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 5:13).
and turns it over in the mikveh. So that the water enters the entire interior of the vessel, as explained above, 3:12.
and lifts it out by its bottom, etc.. He turns it back and removes the pot with its bottom side facing up, so that no water enters it while it is being removed (see also above, 5:3).
a mikveh whose water is shallow. It contains forty se'ah, but the water does not cover the person immersing because the level is low.

even bundles of straw and bundles of reeds. He may place even something that water passes through, such as straw and reeds, for this water too joins to make up the forty se'ah, and certainly he may place stones (Rash, Mikva'ot 7:7).
until the water piles up higher. So that the water gathers in a confined area and the level rises.
there are six levels among mikva'ot. Different degrees of purity.
the first. The lowest level.
pooled water. Water that gathered in a hollow in the ground.
pits, ditches and caves. Different kinds of excavations in the ground.
only if willingly. Only if the impurity touched the water with the person's willing intent.
as we explained. Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 15:1.

they are presumed pure. We must assume that impurity did not touch them by a person's willing intent (and this refers to the rainy season or a place where there is no concern that people walked there; see there, halachot 2-3).

to make dough from them that is subject to challah. To knead with them dough from which challah will be separated for the kohen, who eats it in purity (but they are not fit for the challah itself or for terumah, out of concern that they became impure willingly; see the next halacha).
as will be explained. Below 11:1, that drawn water purifies the hands only through pouring from a vessel.
water of tamtzit. Water that was squeezed out from rain falling on the mountains and gathered together.
for the rains have not stopped but are still falling and the mountains are oozing. The mountains are still seeping and releasing water from the rains falling on them.

and they flow and gather. The water flows and collects in one place. And because it is in the ground and the water keeps flowing to it, it does not become impure even by a person's willing intent (Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 15:6, Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 1:6).
they are fit for terumah. Since this water does not become impure at all, there is no concern that it became impure and it is fit for terumah (and also for challah, whose law is like terumah).

and one may immerse in them water that became impure. Although they do not contain forty se'ah and do not purify a person or vessels, nevertheless they purify impure water (for impure water is purified in a mikveh, Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 2:21).
one who digs beside the sea. A pit into which water flows from the sea.
it is like tamtzit water that has not stopped. Since the flow from the source continues constantly.
as long as it comes by the force of the spring. That the water flows into the pit by the force of the gushing of the spring.
that stop and resume flowing. The flow stops because of a temporary obstruction and afterward resumes.
like spring water. Which is of a high level of purity, as explained later in the chapter.
they are like pooled water. Like the law of tamtzit water that has stopped.
a mikveh that contains, etc.. Forty se'ah of rainwater that gathered in one place in the ground.
except for a male zav. Who must immerse in a spring of living water, as below, halacha 8.
as we explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 8:7, that the hands are purified for holy things only by immersion and not by washing.
the spring. Gushing water.
whose water is little. That does not cover the person immersing.

it is the same as a mikveh, etc.. Its law is like rainwater with regard to the law of 'zochalin' (flowing water): rainwater purifies only when it rests in one place ('ashboran'), and not when it is flowing (unlike a spring, which purifies even when flowing, as below, halachot 7-8).
and it is the same as a spring, etc.. Its law is like gushing water with regard to purification in less than forty se'ah.
even any amount purifies. When the water covers the person immersing.
damaged. Defective.
living water. Fresh water (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 1:8).
in which alone male zavim immerse. See also above, 1:5.

and from which they take for the purification of the leper. For the purification of a leper one must take living water in a vessel and slaughter into it one of the leper's birds and then sprinkle on the leper (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:1).

and to sanctify sin-offering waters. For the purification of one impure from a corpse, one must take living water in a vessel and put into it ashes of the red heifer and sprinkle on the impure person (Hilchot Parah 6:1). For all of these things the Torah says 'living water' (see Leviticus 14:5-6, 15:13, Numbers 19:17).
in ashboran. When the water is gathered and stationary in one place.
the trough. A vessel from which animals drink.
and what is outside the trough. That flows onward after leaving the trough.

invalid. Like the law of drawn water (and although they are connected to the spring and the spring has the power to validate them, nevertheless the Sages treated them as drawn; see Rash, Mikva'ot 5:1, Rosh, Hilchot Mikva'ot sec. 9).

if some of the water flowed over the lip of the trough, etc.. When much water flows into the trough and some of it passes over the side of the vessel and does not enter it, that water does not become drawn and even purifies the water that was in the trough and flowed out.
that pool is like a mikveh. The spring water no longer has the status of a spring because it mixed with the pool's water and was held there, contrary to the nature of a spring whose waters flow.
if it was flowing out of the pool. If the spring water flows out of the pool and continues flowing onward on the other side of the pool.
this is invalid, etc.. The water in the pool, which is a mixture of spring water and rainwater, has the law of a spring, but it is not considered living water.
until he knows that they have gone out, etc.. If it is known that all the rainwater has already gone out, and the water now present is only spring water, it is considered living water.

it is like a mikveh, provided that he does not immerse on top of the vessels. The Sages forbade immersing on top of a vessel even though it has no receptacle and the water on it is not drawn, as a decree lest he immerse inside a vessel that has a receptacle. And since they forbade immersing there, the water that flows from the spring and continues onward after the vessel is considered disconnected from the spring and has the law of mikveh water (Galot Iliyot, Mikva'ot 5:2).
channels. Canals.
until the water in the channels grew strong and flooded. The addition of drawn water caused the flow of the water to strengthen.
they are like a spring for all purposes. Because the spring water was flowing even before the drawn water was added.

they are equal to a mikveh to purify only in ashboran, etc.. Because their flowing is not by the force of the spring but by the force of the drawn water, and their law is that of a spring whose waters are few and to which drawn water was added (above, halacha 6).
they purify when flowing and are invalid for zavim, etc.. Sea water is considered gushing water, but it is not living water.
and those that drip from the spring. For example, where the spring is at the top of a mountain and drops fall from it on the slopes of the mountain.
even though they hurry. Even though the drops fall in a rush one after another.

they are like a mikveh. The water that accumulates from the drops has the law of a mikveh, because the flow from the spring is not in a continuous stream and the connection to the spring is cancelled.
he must surround with a mat, etc.. To surround with a mat the water in which he immerses in order to hold it in one place.

drippings that he made flow, etc.. Water that drips from a spring at the top of a mountain, from which the law of spring has been cancelled as mentioned in the previous halacha, can be restored to the law of a spring by placing a flat vessel that does not become impure (such as a clay board), which turns the dripping into a continuous flow, and thereby the water that accumulates from this flow is connected to the spring.
that he channeled over walnut leaves. He directed them over the outer green husks of the walnut, which have a receptacle (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eduyot 7:4).

for moist walnut leaves, which are used for dyeing, are not considered vessels. Since the moist walnut leaf, which is used as a dye, is not considered a vessel because it is meant for dyeing with it (Levush, Yoreh De'ah 201).
the immersion did not take effect for them. For their outer side was immersed in flowing water and not in stationary water.

if it contains forty se'ah, they are pure for chullin. Although the wave comes from the sea, which has the law of a spring that purifies in any amount, nevertheless forty se'ah are required, since the wave was torn from the sea and the law of the sea was cancelled for it, and since the person or the vessels stand in place and the wave falls on them, it counts as immersion in ashboran (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 4:5).
in Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot. 13:2.
for the thing he intended. For tithe, or terumah, or holy things.
because one may not immerse in flowing water. For before the wave falls to the ground it is flowing, and since it was torn from the sea it no longer purifies by flowing (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 4:5).

all the more so in the air. Not only is the wave flowing, but it is also disconnected from the ground and in the air, and immersion in the air is not effective even when the wave is not flowing, as explained immediately below.

if the two ends of the wave touched the ground, etc.. In this case the wave has the law of ashboran, and nevertheless one may not immerse in its upper part (the 'arch') because it is in the air (there).
a doubt about drawn water, which the Sages declared pure. As stated in Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 14:1.

its doubt is pure because he has something to rely on. It is possible to assume that the drawn water fell into the complete mikveh and its falling caused no invalidity at all, and thus, because of the doubt, the deficient mikveh remains valid.

where he has nothing to rely on: if it fell into this one it is invalidated, etc.. Since the two mikva'ot are in the same situation and there is no preference to assume that the drawn water fell into one of them, both are invalid.
a mikveh that he left empty. A valid mikveh that was emptied of its water.
to this mikveh. To the mikveh presumed valid.
and the mortar. A pounding vessel.
a doubt whether it was from the pipe to the mikveh or from the mortar to the mikveh. Doubt whether the water fell directly from the pipe into the mikveh or first passed through the mortar.
for the invalid one proves. Since the mortar is placed beside it.
and if the mikveh contains a majority of valid water. That it contained the majority of forty se'ah of valid water before the water fell into it from the pipe beside which the mortar stands.

it is valid, for this is a doubt about drawn water, since there is a fixed valid mikveh there. Since the mikveh contained a majority of valid water, it is like a mikveh presumed valid (even though it does not contain forty se'ah), and a doubt about drawn water does not invalidate it. For although the prohibition of drawn water is rabbinic and a rabbinic doubt is resolved leniently, nevertheless one who immerses in a mikveh has a presumption of impurity (as below, halacha 6), and therefore he can be removed from his presumption only when the doubt concerns a mikveh presumed valid (Chazon Ish, Mikva'ot 2:1).
mikva'ot that are found. Whose validity is not known.
in cities. In towns.
inside the key. On the inner side of the town gate.

for the people of the town wash clothes in them and constantly pour drawn water into them. There is concern that they washed their clothes in the mikveh and made it drawn water, or that from the start it was filled with drawn water (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 8:1).
for the impure remains in his presumption. He stays in his current status.

whether the mikveh was in the public domain, etc.. Regarding a doubt of impurity there is a distinction between the public domain, where we are lenient, and the private domain, where we are strict (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 15:8). But in our halacha the subject is a doubt of purity, that is, doubt whether the impure person was purified, and in this there is no distinction (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 2:2).

all the pure items that were made on it, etc.. All things that were presumed pure on the basis of immersion in this mikveh during the time that passed since the previous measurement, in which the mikveh was found complete, are impure.
from severe impurity. One who became impure with a primary source of impurity (by Torah law or rabbinic law; see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 15:1).
but if he immersed from light impurity, such as one who ate impure foods, etc.. These impurities are derivatives of impurity of rabbinic origin (see there 8:10; 9:1).
as we explained. There 15:1.
and one invalid. Invalidated by the falling in of three logs of drawn water (Mercheret HaMishneh).
and made pure things. He handled pure terumah.

these are in suspense. Impure out of doubt, for there is doubt about the immersion from severe impurity (as above, halacha 6). Their law is that they are not eaten, lest they be impure, and not burned, lest they be pure, for it is forbidden to burn pure terumah.
and the second ones are pure. For before he touched them he immersed in both mikva'ot and certainly became pure.
and if these touched those. If the first pure items touched the second ones.

the first are in suspense and the second are burned. The second pure items are certainly impure: for if the first immersion was in the invalid mikveh, the first pure items became impure with severe impurity and make the second impure by touching them, and if the second immersion was in the invalid mikveh, the person came in with his head and most of his body in drawn water and is impure with light impurity and makes the second pure items impure by touching them (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 9:1). But the first remain in suspense because contact with the second does not change their status, for even if the second immersion was in the invalid mikveh, the second items became impure with light impurity and count as a third-degree impurity (see there), and do not make the first impure (Kesef Mishneh in the name of Rash, Mikva'ot 2:2).

and likewise if he became impure in between, etc.. In this case too the first remain in suspense in any event, and the second are pure out of doubt if they did not touch the first. For if the second immersion was in the valid mikveh, the second are pure, and if the second immersion was in the invalid mikveh, the second became impure from the light impurity of the person, and with a doubt about light impurity one is lenient, as stated in the previous halacha (but if the second touched the first, the second are impure in any event, either because they became impure from the person's light impurity or because they became impure by touching the first).

the first are pure. For if the first immersion was in the valid mikveh they are pure, and if it was in the invalid mikveh they are impure with light impurity, and a doubt about light impurity is resolved leniently.
and the second are in suspense. For if the second immersion was in the valid mikveh they are pure, and if it was in the invalid mikveh they are impure with severe impurity.
the first are burned and the second remain in suspense as they were. The first are certainly impure (either with light impurity or by touching the second), but the second are doubtfully impure.

one who immerses from severe impurity, his pure items are in suspense, etc.. When there is doubt whether the immersion was valid, we are strict regarding severe impurity and lenient regarding light impurity (as above, halacha 6).
one was impure. With severe impurity.
to cool off. To cool off for his enjoyment.
as we explained. In the previous paragraph.
and this one who went down to cool off is pure as he was. And we do not say that he became impure on the doubt that he came with his head and most of his body into drawn water.

for this is a doubt about drawn water: perhaps he immersed in the drawn water when he cooled off and became impure. Doubt whether he became impure because he entered drawn water or perhaps he immersed in a valid mikveh and did not become impure at all, and his law is as above at the end of halacha 6.
of twenty se'ah each. Each containing twenty se'ah.
these are pure. Because of the doubt.

these are burned, etc.. For even if the second immersion was in the valid mikveh, it does not contain forty se'ah, and thus the person did not become pure from the first immersion in the drawn mikveh.
as we explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 9:1, where they decreed impurity for this.
we have already explained. Hilchot Berachot 6:2, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 8:7-8.
and immersion of the hands. In order to purify them for holy things, but for terumah washing suffices (there).
and by the force of a giver. Through an act of pouring, and not that the water pours on its own.
in Hilchot Berachot. 6:6, 6:11-14.
anything that interposes in immersion. As detailed above in chapter 2.
and anything that rises to the measure of the mikveh like spat mud. See above 7:3.
he must rub. His hands against each other (Commentary on the Mishnah, introduction to Tractate Yadayim), to remove all the dirt from them (Mishnah Berurah, Orach Chayim 162, subsection 24).

and these are called the first waters; they became impure on his hands. The first waters purify the hands but become impure themselves (for a liquid touching impure hands becomes first-degree impure, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 8:10), and therefore the Sages ordained washing a second time in order to remove from the hands the remnants of water that became impure (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yadayim 2:2). And included in the ordinance is that the first waters do not make the second impure and also do not make the hands impure again, for otherwise it would be impossible to purify hands (Tosafot Yom Tov there).

for the second waters do not purify, etc.. The second waters are meant to remove the first waters that remained on the back of his hands and became impure because of them, and they do not purify the hands themselves.
the hands become impure and are purified up to the joint. See also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 8:1.
up to the joint. The place of connection between limbs or parts of limbs is called a joint; for the identification of the joint mentioned here see Piskei VeShitot.
and poured the second waters outside the joint. Up to the joint and also beyond it.

for the first waters outside the joint became impure from his hand. Although the part of the arm beyond the joint is not included in the impurity of the hands, nevertheless the first waters beyond the joint became impure because they first touched the palm and afterward went out beyond the joint.

and the second waters do not purify water outside the joint. For purification through second waters is a special ordinance in the law of washing hands, and was instituted only regarding water falling on the part of the hand that requires washing (up to the joint).
he poured the first waters on one hand. Because he wanted to purify only it.

and changed his mind and poured the second waters on both hands. He regretted and decided to purify both hands, and poured the second waters on both hands together (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yadayim 2:3).
he washed one hand and rubbed it against its fellow, etc.. Even if he washed it also with second waters and it was fully purified, it becomes impure again when it touches its fellow.
he rubbed it on his head or on the wall. Which are not impure.
four or five. People, for all the hands count as one hand (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yadayim 2:3).
that they be loose. That the hands be relaxed and not pressed against one another.
it is impure as it was. For there is no washing in halves; rather he must wash the entire hand at once (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yadayim 1:1).
wet enough to wet others. Water in such quantity that an item touching the water can wet a third item.
it is pure. For the two stages in this washing count as one washing.
but with the second. Which do not purify but only remove the first (below, halacha 8).
revi'it. A quarter of a log, about 86 cc.
for two hands. One revi'it for both hands of a person.
as we explained regarding washing hands for bread. Hilchot Berachot 6:4, 6:10.
he took from all. From the mixture of the valid and invalid.
and only a revi'it remained as it was. In the amount it was at the beginning.
by another's force. By the force of a person who pours (the washer himself or another person), and as above, halacha 1.
the waters invalid for washing hands and the valid. Halachot 7-9.
and all the vessels with which one washes, etc.. Halachot 11-12.
and what is giving by the force of a giver, etc.. Halachot 13-14.
as we explained there. Halacha 15.

he immersed and was not presumed, it is as if he did not immerse. If he immersed and did not intend that through the immersion he be presumed pure for terumah or holy things, he is not purified for them (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 13:2; but for chullin, immersion without intent is effective after the fact, as above 1:8).
and bad dispositions. Bad character traits.
